t: Minimum Area Rectangle II — Diagonal Pairing
o: We must find four of the given points that form a rectangle (any orientation) and return the smallest area, or 0 if none exists. A quadrilateral is a rectangle iff its two diagonals are equal in length and share the same midpoint. In example 1, the four points form a tilted square whose diagonals both have length sqrt(2) centered at (1,1), giving area 2. In example 2, an axis-aligned unit square exists, so the answer is 1. In example 3 no four points satisfy the condition, so we return 0. With n <= 50, even O(n^4) brute force (~6M checks) is feasible, but grouping by (center, diagonal length) gives a cleaner O(n^3)-ish solution.
k: A quadrilateral is a rectangle iff its diagonals are congruent and bisect each other (same midpoint).
Group point pairs by (midpoint, squared length); any two pairs in the same group form a rectangle.
Use squared distances to avoid floating-point errors in comparisons; only compute area with sqrt at the end.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over All Quadruples
a.i: Try every combination of 4 points and check whether they form a rectangle. For an ordered check, take three points p1,p2,p3 as a corner and adjacent vertices: verify right angle at p1 via dot product, then compute the fourth corner p1+p3-p2 and confirm it exists in the set. This directly tests the rectangle property using vectors.
s: Put all points in a hash set for O(1) lookup.
For each ordered triple (p1,p2,p3), check that vectors p1->p2 and p1->p3 are perpendicular (dot product 0) and nonzero.
Compute candidate fourth corner p4 = p2 + p3 - p1; if it exists in the set, compute area = |p1p2| * |p1p3|.
Track the minimum area; return it (or 0).
a.t: O(n^3) with the hash-set trick (fixing a corner and two neighbors determines the fourth point), effectively constant per triple; worst-case O(n^4) if written as pure quadruple enumeration.

a.n: Approach 2: Group Pairs by Center and Diagonal Length
a.i: Every rectangle's two diagonals share the same midpoint and have equal length. So enumerate all O(n^2) point pairs, key each pair by (midpoint, squared length), and store them in a map. Any two distinct pairs sharing a key form a rectangle; its sides can be recovered from the pair endpoints, so the area is simply dist(p1,p3) * dist(p2,p4) where the two pairs are (p1,p2) and (p3,p4).
s: Build a map from key (cx, cy, d2) to a list of point pairs, where (cx,cy) is the doubled midpoint and d2 the squared length.
Enumerate all unordered pairs of points and append them to their key's list.
For each list, compare every pair of entries (p1,p2) and (p3,p4): compute area = dist(p1,p3) * dist(p1,p4) (the two diagonals cross at the shared center).
Track the minimum area across all groups; return 0 if none found.
a.t: O(n^2) to build groups plus O(sum m_g^2) to match pairs within groups, which is O(n^3) worst case but typically far less; hashing dominates.
a.sp: O(n^2) for storing all point pairs grouped by diagonal key.

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 (right-angle + fourth-corner lookup) since it is easy to reason about, then mention the diagonal-grouping insight as the elegant optimization. Pitfalls: comparing floating-point midpoints/lengths exactly — use doubled integer coordinates and squared lengths as keys; forgetting degenerate zero-length sides; returning 0 when no rectangle exists. Edge cases include fewer than 4 points (answer 0) and collinear-only inputs. Follow-ups might ask for rectangles with sides parallel to axes (LeetCode 939, solvable in O(n^2)), counting all rectangles instead of minimum area, or handling duplicate points.
